lines.text: 3.2 What Is Food Made Of?
ag NARRATIVE
Aarav skips breakfast on Wednesday. By the second period he cannot follow
what the teacher is saying, and by the third his hands feel unsteady. At break,
Ira gives him half a banana. Within a few minutes he feels roughly human again.
Half a banana. A few minutes. Something in that banana reached his blood
fast enough to change how he felt in class.
CONCEPT
Something in food, then, is not the same as food. When we eat a banana we are
not eating "banana" as far as the body is concerned. We are eating a mixture of
substances, each of which the body uses for a different job. These substances are
the components of food.
Different foods carry different components in different amounts. That is why no
single food keeps a person well, and why the mixture on the plate matters as much
as the items on it.
Start with the component that rescued Aarav.
Carbohydrates
Glucose is the simplest sugar the body runs on, and it is a carbohydrate.
Carbohydrates are the body's main source of quick energy. This is why a marathon
runner drinks glucose water during a race rather than eating a meal: glucose needs
almost no processing before the muscles can use it.
We rarely eat pure glucose. We eat carbohydrates in the form of cereals — wheat,
rice, maize, jowar; in root vegetables — potato and sweet potato; and in fruits —
banana, mango, pineapple, sugarcane. Ordinary table sugar is a carbohydrate too.
